source: Coulson and Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an ERP study
finding: Readers saw sentence-final words used literally, as a 'literal mapping' (literal word, but the context prompts mapping from another domain), or metaphorically. N400 size grew in that order. This is the main human test that blending-style mapping effort has a measurable cost, even for literal text.
numbers: N=18 adults. Order literal < literal mapping < metaphor on N400 (300-500 ms): sentence main effect F(2,34)=3.90, p<.05; metaphor vs literal F(1,17)=6.86, p<.02; literal mapping did not differ significantly from either (F=2.03, F=2.18). Linear trend carried over 98% of sentence-type variance. Metaphors also gave a larger posterior positivity. Comprehension accuracy at least 84% for all, mean 91% (SD 4%). Cloze norming with 80 people; 26% of trials rejected.
quote: literal mappings elicited an N400 of intermediate amplitude
limits: Small N, one language, one stimulus set. A graded N400 shows integration cost, but cloze and semantic-fit accounts are only partly controlled. It does not show that blends improve any answer, nor that the four-space steps are what the brain does.
agent_relevance: Combining two frames has a real cost that grows with how far apart the frames are. Argues for budgeting extra steps on distant combinations (O7), not treating all combinations alike.

source: Coulson and Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an ERP study (rival accounts and weak pairwise tests)
finding: The N400 gradient is also what a graded semantic-integration or cloze account would predict, so the result fits blending but does not single it out. Pairwise tests between neighbouring conditions were small.
numbers: Literal mapping vs metaphor and vs literal: both F below 2.2, not significant. Metaphoricity ratings: metaphors rated more metaphoric than literals F(1,17)=612.0, p<.0001, and than literal mappings F(1,17)=451.7, p<.0001; literal mappings rated more metaphoric than literals F(1,17)=38.9, p<.001. Posterior positivity: sentence x anterior/posterior F(8,136)=16.8, p<.001.
limits: Telling blending apart from salience-imbalance, career-of-metaphor or relevance accounts needs different designs. This paper does not supply them.
agent_relevance: A result that 'fits blending' is weak evidence for the exact step sequence. Do not copy the step list into the schema on this ground alone.

source: Glebkin (2013) A critical view on conceptual blending theory
finding: Critique in the CogSci proceedings. Says Fauconnier and Turner's flagship examples (Buddhist monk, Debate with Kant, Regatta, computer desktop, complex numbers) mostly compress known structure into a form lay people can hold, rather than create new knowledge. Says the theory 'did not rest on any experimental data'.
numbers: No new data. Names five earlier objectors: Gibbs 2000, Harder 2003, Brandt 2005, Oakley and Hougaard 2008, Ferguson and Sanford 2008. The three-phase scheme (composition, completion, elaboration) is from Fauconnier and Turner 1998, p.144.
quote: The model described, however, did not rest on any experimental data
limits: Conceptual critique with a cultural-historical (Vygotsky) bent. The complex-number argument is the author's own reading. No test of whether blends give better solutions.
agent_relevance: The best-known blends are explanations given after the fact. Treat 'blend' as a way to present or compress, and require an external check before treating a blend as new knowledge (G3).

source: Glebkin (2013) reading of counterfactual studies (de Vega et al. 2007; Ferguson and Sanford 2008; de Vega and Urrutia 2011)
finding: Reports that counterfactual-comprehension experiments cut against the strict order composition, then completion, then elaboration. Background knowledge is held from the start, and blend elements are first treated as elements of the real world, then reassigned to the counterfactual space.
numbers: Second-hand. De Vega et al. 2007 as described: probe words from the story start were verified faster after counterfactual than factual stories (lottery and Mercedes story). Ferguson and Sanford 2008: anomalies in factual and counterfactual contexts meet similar obstacles at first, and counterfactual topology is used only at a second stage. No effect sizes given.
limits: Numbers are not given in this source and the primary papers were not opened. Treat as a lead, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: If real processing is not stepwise, a coded pipeline is a design choice, not a model of the mind. Keep the steps only if they pay on tests.

source: Ritchie (2004) Lost in space: metaphors in conceptual integration theory (hosted copy, read via summariser)
finding: Argues the four-space layout comes from the 'space' and 'blend' metaphors, not from evidence. Says existing evidence fits blending but does not tell it apart from rivals, and that the model needs a stopping rule because human interpretation varies with haste, involvement and need for cognition. Offers activation and suppression network accounts, and ordinary memory use, as simpler explanations of the examples.
numbers: No experiments. Cites Gibbs 2000, 2001 (not testable as stated), Veale and O'Donoghue 2000 (a program can produce results consistent with the 1998 model), Harder 2003 (children separate colour from apparent colour near age four; Ritchie disputes the task).
limits: Read through a summariser, so exact wording is not verified. Conceptual critique only.
agent_relevance: Matches our rule G1: a combine step needs a stop condition and a trigger. 'Run until it feels right' is not a rule.

source: Gibbs (2000) Making good psychology out of blending theory (as reported by Ritchie, Glebkin and Wikipedia)
finding: Main critique: the framework is not stated so it can be tested or falsified; many separate hypotheses would be needed; inferring process from products is shaky; other theories explain the same cases.
numbers: No numbers. Fauconnier and Turner (2002) replied by adding governing principles (topology, integration, 'achieve human scale').
limits: Original paper not opened. Secondary descriptions only; Wikipedia, Ritchie and Glebkin agree on the gist.
agent_relevance: Any claim that blending helps an agent must be tested on our own tasks, with a no-blend control. The theory will not supply the prediction.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026) Conceptual blending
finding: Overview page lists no empirical studies with numbers. Lists computational work: Shrager (view application, 1987 and 1990), Guhe et al. 2011 (basic mathematics), Lieto and Pozzato 2019 and 2020 (typicality logic for concept combination).
numbers: Zero quantitative evaluations on the page.
limits: Encyclopedia, not a primary source. Useful only for pointers.
agent_relevance: Most computational blending work was judged by example, not by a benchmark. See the computational-blending subfield.

source: Privative-adjective MEG/EEG study (2026, Imaging Neuroscience; builds on Fritz and Baggio 2020). 'Fake gun' is the Coulson and Fauconnier (1999) blending case
finding: Pre-registered study of adjective-noun phrases: privative adjectives (fake, the classic blending example) against subsective ones (bad). Privative phrases were verified less accurately, as a blending-cost view predicts. The authors cite Fritz and Baggio 2020 for more negative potentials at 500-800 ms for privative phrases.
numbers: N=36 adults (27 women), native English, power-planned with G*Power. Accuracy: denotation main effect chi2=22.49, p<.0001; privative less accurate than single-word controls (OR -2.61, p=.004) and than subsective phrases (OR -4.48, p<.0001); subsective vs baseline not significant (p=.20). Concrete phrases faster (1.52 s) than abstract (1.74 s). Decoding: noun concreteness generalised better to subsective than privative phrases.
limits: The cost of 'fake X' could come from negation or type-shifting, not blending. The study did not test blend-specific predictions. Fritz and Baggio 2020 itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Modifiers that cancel a property (fake, former) are error-prone for humans and probably for models. A combine step should list which properties were cancelled.

source: Zacharakis, Kaliakatsos-Papakostas, Kalaitzidou, Cambouropoulos (2021) Evaluating human-computer co-creative processes in music (CHAMELEON)
finding: A harmonisation tool that blends two musical idioms (by averaging transition probabilities) was tested with composers and students. With the tool, people made more complex, diverse and unexpected harmonisations than a control group, and novices liked the tool more than professionals did.
numbers: Main experiment N=25 (20 students, rest composers); extra control group of novices without the tool. Overall Creativity Index: no group difference without the tool (z=-2, p=0.051); with the tool composers lower than students (z=2.31, p=0.042, effect size 0.33, median diff 1.08). Mean index: composers 5.8 then 4.7, students 5.57 then 5.6. Students rated it easier to express ideas (z=-2.2, p=0.028) but harder and harder to concentrate. No Bonferroni correction; with it no effect survives.
limits: Small N, no independent quality rating of the outputs, multiple uncorrected tests. Shows more diverse output, not better output. Expertise reversed the tool's appeal.
agent_relevance: A blend operator widens the option set; it does not by itself make answers correct. Pair with a code selector. Expect strong baselines to gain less.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: A GPT-3 plus knowledge-base tool suggests blends between a product and a pop-culture domain. About 56% of suggested connecting concepts were judged accurate per strategy, yet over 90% of pairs had at least one good concept among five. In a within-subject study people found over twice as many blends with the tool.
numbers: Annotation: average accuracy of connecting concepts 56.0%, 55.3%, 58.7% (No-GPT, Half-GPT, Full-GPT); at least one of five correct 90.0%, 96.6%, 93.3%. Stage 2: product scenes related 89.1% vs pop-culture scenes 75.9%. GPT-3 attribute accuracy 2.86 of 5 (57%); adjectives 79%, activities 58%, catchphrases 35%; rater agreement 0.32 to 0.47. User study N=10: 2.03 (SD 0.84) vs 0.87 (SD 0.56) blends per pair, Wilcoxon p<0.001; mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80 (p=0.004); effort 3.05 vs 5.00 (p=0.006).
limits: N=10 amateur designers, five minutes per pair, baseline was web search. GPT-3 (2021) only. Counts ideas, not quality. About 4 in 10 suggestions were wrong, so a check is needed.
agent_relevance: Generate-many-then-filter works: any one suggestion is wrong about 44% of the time, but a set of five almost always has a good one. Fits a code-side selector over several blend proposals.

source: Sun et al. (2025) Creative Blends of Visual Concepts
finding: A system maps an abstract idea to concrete objects through metaphor (commonsense base plus an LLM), then blends the objects in an image. In a within-subject study it lowered workload and raised creativity-support scores against a baseline.
numbers: N=24 (12 female, 12 male), Latin-square order. Usability (SUS): paired t(23)=-2.547, p=0.018, Cohen's d=0.800. Mental demand t(23)=4.861, p<0.001; physical demand Z=-2.865, p=0.004; effort t(23)=2.734, p=0.012. Creativity Support Index: exploration t(23)=-2.985, p=0.007; collaboration t(23)=-3.350, p=0.003; enjoyment t(23)=-3.558, p=0.002. Formative interviews with 8 participants.
limits: Subjective ratings; no independent expert grading of blend quality in the parts read. Visual domain. Baseline was a conversational image tool.
agent_relevance: Evidence of lower effort and more exploration, not of correct answers. Useful for open design tasks only.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and inducing combinational creativity in vision-language models (CreativeMashup, IEI framework)
finding: Maps blending to three levels: identify the two inputs, explain shared attributes, derive implication. On 666 expert-made visual mashups the best vision-language models beat average humans at understanding but not experts. Prompting through all three levels before generating images beat prompting with identification and implication only.
numbers: Implication task winning rate: human experts 78.3%, GPT-4o 73.5%, GPT-4V 71.9%, Gemini-1.5-Pro 71.7%, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 62.9%, average humans 51.0%, Claude-3-Opus 39.2%, LLaVA-1.5-7B 20.1%. Identification precision/recall: GPT-4o 75.67/85.00, average humans 53.42/70.33. Generation: 50 Prolific raters; mean rank IEI 1.98 vs II 2.40 (lower is better; expert-made images ranked best). Prompt length did not differ significantly; in 46.0% of cases where IEI won, its prompt was shorter. GPT-4o judge agreed with two experts 85.1% and 81.6% on 200 comparisons.
limits: Images, not reasoning. The judge is GPT-4o, so own-model bias is possible. Gains were larger for stronger models; Stable Diffusion 3 gained little. Authors credit the Explanation step (shared attributes) for the gain.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of a stepwise blend prompt. Naming shared structure before combining helped, and not because of length. Supports a generic-space step before a combine step.

source: Schapiro et al. (2025/2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in LLMs and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Benchmark of association, analogy and blending across 35 LLMs and 75 humans. Blending is hardest. The bottleneck is not building the blend; it is finding a valid shared abstraction (generic space) first.
numbers: LLMs valid on average: association 59.0%, analogy 53.4%, blend 43.4% (10 to 16 points lower on blends). Given a valid generic space, models describe a coherent blend 97.1% of the time; they find a valid generic space only 43.4% of the time. Humans (N=75 Prolific, mean age 40.1): association 22.1%, analogy 32.9%, blend 12.8%. Cross-task model correlations r=0.71 (association-analogy), 0.70, 0.54 (all p<0.001). Top model gpt-5.6-sol 64.8% on blending vs 55.4% on analogy.
limits: Validity judged by a three-judge LLM panel that agreed with humans 75% of the time on unanimous items. Humans scored lower mainly on utility, so the human-LLM gap is partly effort and task format.
agent_relevance: Direct support for an explicit generic-space step with a code check on it (is the abstraction true of both inputs?). Without it blends fail at the first hurdle.

source: Schapiro et al. (2025/2026) KOMBINE: homogeneity of invented concepts
finding: When models invent a concept by recombining parts, they reuse each other's ideas, more so on blends than on analogies, and more within one provider.
numbers: 19.9% of invented concepts (412 of 2,070) reuse a property invented by another model at the loosest threshold; models are 14 times more likely to reuse properties on blends than on analogies; same-provider models 2.3 times more likely than different-provider ones. Some providers converge 12.2 and 11.1 points above baseline.
limits: Overlap threshold choices matter. Measures reuse, not quality.
agent_relevance: Blend samples from one model are correlated (matches G4). More samples from the same model add less diversity than expected; vary the inputs or frames instead.

source: Schapiro et al. (2025/2026) KOMBINE: failure analysis of blends
finding: Typical blend failure: the generic space applies to only one input (for example, air spaces in photosynthesis are not made by gas exchange), so the blend is incoherent from the start.
numbers: Invalid generic space was the main failure type; valid blend given a valid generic space 97.1%. Humans also found blending the hardest of the three tasks.
limits: Qualitative cases; per-category counts not extracted by this agent.
agent_relevance: Add a code-run test: state the shared structure, then check that each input satisfies it, before elaboration.

source: Sato (2025) The way we prompt: conceptual blending, neural dynamics and prompt-induced transitions in LLMs
finding: Review that maps blending onto LLM prompting and names two effects: prompt-induced transition (shifts in tone or meaning) and prompt-induced hallucination (plausible but ungrounded output from fusing distant domains, such as periodic table plus tarot).
numbers: No quantitative results in the text read (8 pages, no tables of rates or tests). Examples are single prompts.
limits: Anecdotal and interpretive. Says CBT's 'experimental and neural validation is still emerging'. Not evidence of any gain.
agent_relevance: Warns that fusing far-apart domains yields confident but unfounded text. A blend step needs a grounding check on any new claim (G3).

source: Lynn (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Conceptual analysis: in humans the goal decides which features of each source enter the blend; in LLMs the pull comes from proxy-goals set by the prompt and alignment. Illustrated by a toy vector-symbolic model in Python.
numbers: No measured human or model results. Cites Peng et al. 2025 and Sato 2025 for LLM blending.
limits: Conceptual paper, one author. Claims about brains are proposals, not data.
agent_relevance: Blends need an explicit goal to decide what to project. Pass the task goal into the combine step as the selection rule.

source: Yin (2026) A quantum-cognitive approach to dynamic meaning construction (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Says blending theory 'remains largely descriptive' and offers an interference-based alternative for metaphor and polysemy.
numbers: No blending-specific data in the sections read.
limits: Proposal paper. A rival to blending, not tested against it here.
agent_relevance: Another voice that blending names a result without predicting it. Low weight.

source: Fauconnier and Turner (2002) governing principles as the reply to 'anything goes' (as described by Glebkin 2013 and Wikipedia)
finding: To answer the claim that blending explains any outcome, the authors added governing principles (integration, topology, human scale and others). They are rules of thumb, not computations.
numbers: No numbers. Glebkin notes it is 'not clear' in practice how to decide whether topology is useful.
limits: Book not opened. Principle names come from the Glebkin and Wikipedia texts read.
agent_relevance: If we code a blend operator we must choose concrete scores for each principle and test them. No ready-made weights exist.

source: Status of large replications of human blending experiments (negative finding from this session's search)
finding: From the sources read, no large-sample replication of a blending-specific prediction was found. Experimental work is a handful of small ERP and reading studies (N=18 to 36) showing graded integration cost. No meta-analysis was found.
numbers: Coulson and Van Petten N=18; MEG/EEG privative study N=36; CHAMELEON N=25; PopBlends N=10; Creative Blends N=24. No meta-analysis, pooled effect size or direct failed replication located.
limits: Search was limited: the web search quota ran out and scholarly APIs (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, Crossref) were rate-limited. Absence here is not absence in the literature. Hilpert's mixed-metaphor study, Wilkenfeld and Ward, Estes and Ward, and Hampton's emergent-feature work were not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not call blending 'established' in the schema. Mark it single-source or design choice until our own test.

source: Hilpert (2010) mixed metaphors as a test between metaphor theory and blending (search snippet only)
finding: Snippet says it uses mixed metaphors because Conceptual Metaphor Theory and Blending Theory predict different things, with corpus data and experiments.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Not opened. Lead only; verify before use.
agent_relevance: A rare test that discriminates between rivals. Read it before deciding how blending differs from plain mapping.

source: Schmid, blending and relevance: test of blending's predictive power on noun-noun compounds (search snippet only)
finding: Snippet says the paper sets out to test the predictive power of blending on noun-noun compounds, with relevance theory as the rival.
numbers: No numbers seen; the PDF link redirected and was not read.
limits: Not opened. Lead only.
agent_relevance: Possible source for a direct rival comparison; see the conceptual-combination subfield.

source: Pereira and Cardoso (2003) Divago computational blending, horse plus bird (search snippet only)
finding: Snippet describes a computational horse-bird (Pegasus-style) blending run under optimality constraints.
numbers: No numbers; the link returned 404.
limits: Not opened. Detail belongs to the computational-blending subfield.
agent_relevance: Existing design to copy for a coded operator; read under the sibling subfield.

source: Cross-study pattern in the LLM blending evidence (KOMBINE, IEI, PopBlends, Sato)
finding: In the four LLM studies opened, the step that names shared structure before combining has measured support (IEI explanation step; KOMBINE generic-space bottleneck). Unaided blending of far domains is the weak part (43.4% valid; hallucination examples).
numbers: KOMBINE 43.4% valid generic space and 97.1% coherent blend given one; Peng IEI rank 1.98 vs 2.40; PopBlends 90 to 97% of pairs have at least one good suggestion in five.
limits: Different tasks, judges and models; judges are mostly LLMs or small user samples. No study compared blend prompting with a plain strong-prompt baseline on reasoning accuracy.
agent_relevance: Design lead: generic-space step, code check that both inputs satisfy it, several differently framed attempts, selection by code. Untested as a reasoning gain; needs our own A/B on S3 open mode.

source: Peng et al. (2025) CreativeMashup: fusion versus replacement mashups
finding: Models and people recognised fusion mashups (features merged from both objects) more easily than replacement mashups (one object swapped in for another, with deeper meaning). Replacement needs deeper understanding of why the swap carries meaning.
numbers: Per the text read: fusion showed higher cognition rates than replacement for typical human performance patterns; exact per-type rates were not extracted. Human baseline from Prolific; expert annotation on the same 666 items.
limits: Exact numbers for the split not recorded by this agent. Image domain.
agent_relevance: Single-scope-like swaps (one frame supplies the structure) are easier than double-scope merges. Route far merges through more explicit steps.
